Statement

Consider the sequence \((a_n) = \left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)\). Provve $(a_n) converges to \(L = 1\).

Solution

Let \(L =1\). Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and let \(M = \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\). Suppose \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(n > M\), then \(n > \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\). Since \(n > 0\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\), then \(\frac{1}{n} < \varepsilon\). We compute \[\begin{align*} |a_n - L| &= \left| \frac{n+1}{n} - 1\right|\\ &= \left| \frac{n+1 - n}{n}\right| \\ &= \left| \frac{1}{n} \right|. \end{align*}\] So we have \(|a_n = L | = \frac{1}{n} < \varepsilon\). \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), we have found a real number \(M = \frac{1}{\varepsilon}\) such that for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) if \(n > M\), then \(|a_n - 1| < \varepsilon\). Then \((a_n)\) converges at \(L = 1\). \(\square\)

Solution

Suppose \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \(n > M\), then \(n > \frac{1}{\epsilon}\).

Since \(n > 0\) and \(\epsilon > 0\) then \(\frac{1}{n} < \epsilon\).

\[ |a_n-L| = \left|\frac{n+1}{n}+1\right| = \left|\frac{n+1-n}{n}\right| = \left|\frac{1}{n}\right| \]

\[ |a_n-L| = \frac{1}{n} < \epsilon \]

\(\forall\ \epsilon > 0\), we found a real number \(M = \frac{1}{\epsilon}\) such that all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) if \(n > M\), then \(|a_n-1| < \epsilon\). Then it converges at \(L=1\).
